overview: Safe deployments for data pipelines require a fundamentally different mindset than deploying stateless web services: data pipelines mutate persistent state (tables, partitions, offsets, schema registries), so a bad deploy can corrupt terabytes of data that cannot simply be re-served from the previous container image.

Techniques borrowed from SRE—canary releases, blue-green environments, feature flags, and automated rollback—must be adapted to account for data immutability, schema evolution, late-arriving data, and the need to keep upstream producers and downstream consumers in sync during a transition.

Modern data stacks provide first-class primitives for safe deploys: Iceberg and Delta Lake branches/tags for atomic table swaps, dbt versioned models and environment targets, Airflow DAG serialization and versioned DAG IDs, backward-compatible Avro/Protobuf schema evolution enforced by a schema registry, and CI/CD pipelines that run integration tests against realistic data before any code reaches production.
learningObjectives: Understand why data pipeline deploys are harder to roll back than stateless service deploys and what strategies mitigate that risk.
Implement canary releases for data pipelines by routing a fraction of partitions or tenants through new code and comparing outputs.
Design blue-green table environments with atomic swap primitives (Snowflake SWAP TABLE, BigQuery dataset clone, Iceberg branch, Delta Clone) to achieve zero-downtime schema or logic changes.
Apply backward-compatible schema evolution rules for Avro and Protobuf schemas enforced by a Confluent Schema Registry.
Automate rollback triggers based on data quality regressions, SLA breaches, or output divergence checks.
Version and safely deploy Airflow DAGs and dbt models using environment-targeted builds and blue-green DAG IDs.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Safe data pipeline deployment is the set of practices, primitives, and automated checks that allow changes to pipeline code, schemas, or logic to be released incrementally and verifiably—with the ability to roll back or forward without data loss or consumer disruption—by leveraging atomic table swap operations, backward-compatible schema evolution, canary output comparison, feature-flag-gated code paths, and CI/CD pipelines that validate correctness before promotion to production.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: When you deploy a new version of a web service, rolling back is as simple as swapping a container. Data pipelines are different: they write records to tables, advance Kafka offsets, and evolve schemas. If you deploy bad code that writes wrong data for two hours, rolling back the code does not undo the bad data already written. Safe data deploys are about never letting bad code touch production data at all—or catching the problem so quickly, on so little data, that the damage is easy to undo. Think of it as a bank that lets a teller trainee handle only five transactions under supervision before going solo, while keeping the experienced teller's window open the whole time.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Until roughly 2018, data pipeline deployments were manual, ad-hoc, and high-risk: engineers would log into prod, swap SQL scripts, and pray. The rise of dbt (2016) brought software-engineering discipline—version control, tests, environments—to SQL transformations. Airflow (2014, open-sourced 2015) introduced DAG versioning but its in-place mutation model still caused painful upgrade incidents. Table format innovations (Apache Iceberg 2018, Delta Lake 2019) added ACID transactions, schema evolution, and time travel to lakehouses, making atomic table swaps and point-in-time rollback practical at petabyte scale. Confluent Schema Registry (2015) brought contract enforcement to Kafka schemas. By 2022, teams at Uber, LinkedIn, and Netflix had codified blue-green data deploys and automated rollback runbooks as standard practice.

whyItMatters.business: A bad data pipeline deploy can silently corrupt dashboards, ML feature stores, and financial reports for hours or days before detection; safe deploy practices reduce mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to recover (MTTR) from hours to minutes, protecting downstream business decisions.
whyItMatters.engineering: Canary and blue-green patterns give engineers a safety net that encourages faster iteration: small, frequent, verified changes are less risky than large infrequent deploys, accelerating the team's delivery velocity.
whyItMatters.scalability: Automated output-comparison checks and quality gates scale across hundreds of pipelines and tenants without requiring manual review of every deploy, making safe-deploy discipline maintainable as the platform grows.
whyItMatters.cost: Catching a logic error before it writes 24 hours of corrupted data avoids expensive backfill jobs, analyst investigation time, and customer remediation costs that can easily exceed the savings from skipping safety checks.
whyItMatters.reliability: Encoding rollback triggers as automated quality checks turns 'hope the deploy is correct' into a measurable, enforceable SLO: pipelines are promoted to production only after passing output-divergence and quality thresholds.

coreComponents.name: Canary Release for Data Pipelines
coreComponents.definition: A deployment strategy where new pipeline code processes a small, representative slice of data (a single tenant, date partition, or percentage of Kafka partitions) while old code continues processing the rest, and outputs are compared before the new code is promoted.
coreComponents.purpose: To validate correctness and performance of new pipeline logic on real data at small scale before committing to a full cutover.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Route a subset of input to the new code path, run output-divergence checks comparing canary and baseline outputs, monitor latency and error rates on the canary slice, and either promote or roll back based on comparison results.
coreComponents.examples: Running a new Spark job against a single date partition; routing one Kafka consumer group to new Flink logic while the old group runs in parallel; deploying a new dbt model to a canary schema and comparing row counts and aggregates against the current production model.

coreComponents.name: Blue-Green Data Environments
coreComponents.definition: Maintaining two parallel, identical data environments (blue = current production, green = new version) and performing an atomic swap so consumers are cut over instantaneously without a window of dual-writes or inconsistency.
coreComponents.purpose: To achieve zero-downtime, instantaneous cutover for changes to table structure, ETL logic, or warehouse objects, with an equally instantaneous rollback by swapping back.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Build and validate the green environment completely before the swap, perform the atomic swap using a warehouse-native primitive, keep blue intact for a hold period to allow rollback, and update downstream dependencies to point to the new active name.
coreComponents.examples: Snowflake ALTER TABLE ... SWAP WITH; BigQuery CREATE TABLE ... CLONE followed by renaming datasets; Iceberg branch-and-merge for lakehouse tables; Delta Lake CLONE with atomic table rename.

coreComponents.name: Backward-Compatible Schema Evolution
coreComponents.definition: A set of rules for evolving Avro, Protobuf, or Iceberg/Delta table schemas such that new writers and old readers, or old writers and new readers, can coexist without deserialization errors or data loss.
coreComponents.purpose: To decouple producer and consumer deploy schedules, allowing pipelines to be upgraded independently without coordinated downtime.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Enforce schema compatibility mode in the Confluent Schema Registry (BACKWARD, FORWARD, or FULL), apply only safe schema changes (add nullable columns, add optional Protobuf fields, add Iceberg columns with defaults), and block breaking changes (column renames, type changes, field deletions) at deploy time.
coreComponents.examples: Registering a new Avro schema with BACKWARD compatibility so new consumers can read old messages; adding an optional Protobuf field without breaking existing decoders; adding a nullable column to an Iceberg table without rewriting existing files.

coreComponents.name: Automated Rollback Triggers
coreComponents.definition: Automated checks that continuously monitor pipeline output quality, SLA adherence, and output divergence during and after a deploy, and automatically revert to the previous version when a threshold is breached.
coreComponents.purpose: To remove human latency from the rollback decision and guarantee that data quality regressions are caught and reversed before they propagate to downstream consumers.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Define quality thresholds (null rate, row count delta, aggregate divergence, freshness lag), run checks against each pipeline output after every batch or micro-batch, compare metrics to pre-deploy baselines, and trigger rollback playbooks or Airflow DAG pauses when thresholds are breached.
coreComponents.examples: A Great Expectations suite that gates Airflow task promotion; a dbt test that blocks model publication if row count drops more than 5%; a Flink job that emits a metric to Prometheus and an alert rule that pauses the job and re-enables the previous version.

coreComponents.name: Feature Flags for Pipeline Code
coreComponents.definition: Runtime configuration switches that enable or disable new pipeline code paths without redeploying, allowing gradual rollout and instant kill-switch disablement.
coreComponents.purpose: To separate code deployment from feature activation, enabling code to be merged to main and deployed to production in a dormant state, then enabled for a subset of tenants or partitions before full activation.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Read flag state from a configuration store (LaunchDarkly, AWS AppConfig, environment variable, or a control table in the warehouse) at pipeline start time, branch execution accordingly, log which code path was taken, and update flag state without redeployment.
coreComponents.examples: A PySpark job that reads a feature flag from AWS SSM Parameter Store to decide which transformation branch to execute; an Airflow DAG that checks a control table to skip or include a new task group; a dbt variable (--vars) that switches between model versions.

coreComponents.name: CI/CD for Data Pipelines
coreComponents.definition: Automated pipelines that test, validate, and deploy pipeline code through a series of environments (dev, staging, prod) with quality gates at each stage before promotion.
coreComponents.purpose: To catch logic errors, schema incompatibilities, and performance regressions in automated testing before code reaches production data.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Run unit tests on transformation logic, execute integration tests against realistic sampled data in a staging environment, validate dbt model outputs with automated tests, check schema compatibility against the registry, measure job performance against benchmarks, and deploy only after all gates pass.
coreComponents.examples: A GitHub Actions workflow that runs dbt test on a staging Snowflake environment before merging; a Dockerfile that builds a Spark job and runs pytest against Spark local mode; a Terraform plan that previews infrastructure changes before apply.

internalWorking: Before any production change, the new pipeline version is deployed to a staging or shadow environment where it processes a representative sample of production data (a date partition, a subset of tenants, or a replayed Kafka segment) and its outputs are captured.

Output-divergence checks compare the new version's outputs to the current production version's outputs across key metrics: row counts, aggregate sums, null rates, distribution of key columns, and SLA timestamps. Differences beyond a configurable tolerance threshold block promotion.

For canary releases, traffic splitting is implemented at the partition, tenant, or Kafka partition level. The pipeline orchestrator (Airflow, Prefect, or a Spark job) routes a fraction of input to the new code while the old code handles the rest, and both outputs land in separate namespaced tables.

For blue-green swaps, the green environment (new version) is built completely and validated offline. The swap is executed as a single atomic DDL statement (Snowflake SWAP, BigQuery rename, Iceberg replace) that cuts over consumers instantaneously. The blue environment is retained for a hold period (typically 24–72 hours) to allow quick rollback.

Schema changes are validated before deploy by submitting the new schema to the Confluent Schema Registry compatibility check endpoint. The CI/CD pipeline fails if the schema is not backward compatible, blocking the deploy entirely.

Rollback triggers are implemented as monitoring rules in Prometheus/Grafana or as post-task quality checks in Airflow. When a metric breaches a threshold, an automated runbook (Airflow DAG, AWS Lambda, or PagerDuty webhook) pauses the new pipeline, re-enables the previous version, and pages the on-call engineer.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Code merge to main -> CI runs unit + integration tests + schema compatibility check -> Deploy to staging -> Run canary against single partition + output divergence check -> Gate: quality pass? -> Yes: promote to production blue-green swap (atomic DDL) -> Monitor output quality + SLA for hold period -> Rollback trigger armed: quality breach auto-reverts swap -> Old environment retained for 48h -> Cleanup
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A data engineer opens a PR that changes the revenue attribution logic in a PySpark Spark job. The CI pipeline runs unit tests, executes the job against a 1-day sample in staging, and submits the output Avro schema to the Confluent Schema Registry compatibility check—all must pass before the PR can merge.

2. After merge, the CD pipeline builds a new Docker image, runs a full dbt test suite against the staging Snowflake environment (target: staging), and compares the new model's row count and revenue aggregate to the current production model via a divergence check script. Divergence below 0.1% allows promotion.

3. The pipeline is deployed in canary mode: Airflow routes partition 2024-01-15 through the new Spark job while all other partitions continue with the old job. A post-task comparison DAG runs Great Expectations on both outputs and reports the delta.

4. After 24 hours of clean canary results, the blue-green swap is executed: Snowflake runs ALTER TABLE revenue_attribution_green SWAP WITH revenue_attribution; the old blue table is renamed revenue_attribution_blue_20240115 and retained.

5. Prometheus monitors the post-swap output quality metrics. If null_order_id_rate exceeds 0.5% or row_count drops more than 3% within 2 hours of swap, an alert fires, the swap is automatically reversed by re-running the SWAP statement, and PagerDuty pages the on-call engineer.

keyTerminology.meaning: Routing a small fraction of input data or traffic through new pipeline code while old code handles the rest, then comparing outputs before full cutover.
keyTerminology.importance: Limits blast radius of a bad deploy to a small slice of data rather than the full production dataset.

keyTerminology.meaning: Running two parallel environments (blue = current, green = new), validating green completely, then performing an atomic swap to make green the new production.
keyTerminology.importance: Enables instantaneous, zero-downtime cutover with an equally instant rollback path by swapping back.

keyTerminology.meaning: A single, transactional DDL operation that renames or swaps two tables so consumers see no intermediate state.
keyTerminology.importance: Prevents consumers from reading a partially-built table during a deploy, which could cause incorrect query results.

keyTerminology.meaning: A service (e.g., Confluent Schema Registry) that stores versioned Avro/Protobuf schemas and enforces compatibility rules before a new schema version is registered.
keyTerminology.importance: Prevents breaking schema changes from reaching Kafka topics, decoupling producer and consumer deploy schedules.

keyTerminology.meaning: Automated comparison of a new pipeline version's output against the current production output across key metrics (row counts, aggregates, null rates) to validate correctness before promotion.
keyTerminology.importance: Replaces manual spot-checking with a quantitative, automated correctness gate that scales across many pipelines.

keyTerminology.meaning: Writing pipeline output to both the production destination and a shadow destination simultaneously during a transition, allowing comparison without consumer impact.
keyTerminology.importance: Enables A/B comparison of old and new logic on live data without routing consumers to unvalidated output.

keyTerminology.meaning: A schema change is backward compatible if new readers can deserialize data written by old writers using the new schema (added optional fields, added nullable columns).
keyTerminology.importance: Allows consumers to be upgraded independently of producers without coordinating downtime windows.

keyTerminology.meaning: The practice of assigning explicit version identifiers to Airflow DAGs, running old and new versions in parallel during a cutover window, and retiring the old version after validation.
keyTerminology.importance: Prevents Airflow's in-place DAG mutation from skipping or duplicating runs when code changes mid-pipeline.

importantConcepts.explanation: What: unlike a stateless service where rollback means swapping a container, a data pipeline rollback must also address already-written data. Why: bad pipeline logic can write corrupted records to tables that downstream consumers have already read and acted upon. How: use atomic table swaps so the write target is switched only after validation, or implement dual-write with shadow tables to compare before promotion. Pitfall: treating data pipeline rollback as identical to service rollback leads to incomplete recovery—code is reverted but the data remains corrupted.

importantConcepts.concept: Canary partitioning vs canary traffic splitting
importantConcepts.explanation: What: for batch pipelines, canary is implemented by processing a single date partition or tenant through new code; for streaming pipelines, it is implemented by assigning a subset of Kafka partitions to a new consumer group. Why: both approaches isolate blast radius, but they have different mechanics. How: for Spark batch jobs, override the partition path argument; for Kafka/Flink jobs, configure a dedicated consumer group with a subset of partition assignments. Pitfall: comparing outputs from different time windows or different tenants will produce false positives in the divergence check—always compare structurally equivalent slices.

importantConcepts.concept: Iceberg/Delta branches as code branches for data
importantConcepts.explanation: What: Apache Iceberg's branching API and Delta Lake's CLONE operation allow creating a writeable copy of a table's metadata that can diverge from the main branch and be merged back atomically, analogous to a git branch for data. Why: this enables testing new pipeline logic against a branch of production data without affecting reads from the main branch. How: create a branch with spark.sql('ALTER TABLE prod.orders CREATE BRANCH deploy_test'), write new job output to the branch, validate, and fast-forward merge to main. Pitfall: branches are metadata-only (they share data files) so data written to a branch does consume storage; set TTLs to expire unused branches automatically.

variationsAndTypes: **Partition-level canary (batch):** new Spark/dbt logic runs against one date partition; outputs compared before promoting to all partitions.
**Tenant-level canary (SaaS):** new pipeline logic is enabled for a single low-risk tenant via feature flag; metrics compared before global rollout.
**Kafka partition canary (streaming):** new Flink/Spark Structured Streaming job is assigned a subset of Kafka partitions; old job handles remaining partitions.
**Blue-green warehouse tables:** full new table built under a green name, validated, then swapped atomically with the production name via DDL.
**Blue-green dbt environments:** dbt targets (dev, staging, prod) are separate Snowflake databases; CI promotes a build from staging to prod after test pass.
**Shadow/dual-write:** new pipeline writes output to a shadow table in parallel with the current pipeline; outputs compared without consumer exposure.
**Feature-flagged code path:** new transformation logic is gated by a runtime flag; disabled by default in prod, enabled per-tenant or per-partition for validation.
**Versioned DAG IDs:** Airflow DAGs are named with a version suffix (etl_revenue_v2); old and new run in parallel during a cutover window before the old is paused.
**dbt versioned models:** dbt v1.6+ supports model versions natively; old and new versions of a model coexist in the DAG during migration, with downstream models gradually updated.
advantages: **Drastically reduced blast radius:** canary and feature-flag approaches limit bad deploy impact to a small fraction of data rather than the full production dataset.
**Instantaneous rollback:** atomic table swaps allow reverting a deploy in milliseconds by re-running a single DDL statement, rather than waiting for a backfill.
**Decoupled deploy schedules:** backward-compatible schema evolution allows producers and consumers to deploy independently without coordinated downtime windows.
**Automated quality gates:** output-divergence checks and rollback triggers remove human latency from the rollback decision, catching issues within minutes.
**Confidence through CI/CD:** running integration tests against realistic data in staging before every deploy catches the majority of logic errors before they touch production.
**Auditable deploy history:** versioned DAG IDs, Iceberg snapshots, and dbt run artifacts provide a full audit trail of what ran, when, and what it produced.
disadvantages: **Operational complexity:** blue-green environments double the infrastructure cost during the hold period and require additional orchestration to manage both environments.

**Canary comparison complexity:** defining a meaningful output-divergence check requires understanding which metrics are sensitive indicators and which vary naturally, making initial setup non-trivial.
**Schema registry overhead:** enforcing compatibility modes in a schema registry adds a deploy step and requires team discipline to never bypass the registry.
**Stale blue environment risk:** retaining the blue environment for rollback means it may diverge from upstream data during the hold period, making a rollback more complex than just swapping back.
**Feature flag sprawl:** without governance, feature flags accumulate and become technical debt; old flags that are never cleaned up can obscure the active code path.
**Dual-write cost:** shadow writes double the compute and storage cost during the comparison period.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Apply blue-green or canary deploys for any pipeline that feeds dashboards, ML features, financial reports, or SLA-bound data products. Use schema registry compatibility enforcement for all Kafka-based pipelines with multiple consumers. Invest in output-divergence checks when pipelines are complex enough that logic errors are not immediately obvious from row counts alone.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Skip blue-green environments for internal, non-consumer-facing staging pipelines where a failed deploy can be fixed in place without business impact. Avoid canary partitioning for very small datasets where a single partition is not representative. Skip shadow writes for pipelines where compute cost is the primary constraint and manual sampling review is acceptable.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Safe data pipeline deployment is like a bridge replacement over a live highway. You cannot close the road (stop the pipeline) to rebuild it. Instead, you build the new bridge deck (green environment) alongside the existing one, route a single test vehicle (canary partition) across it and verify structural integrity, then atomically swing the traffic dividers to redirect all vehicles to the new deck (blue-green swap). The old deck is kept intact for 48 hours in case you need to swing traffic back. Only after 48 hours of safe operation do you demolish the old deck (retire the blue environment).

commonMisconceptions.myth: Rolling back a data pipeline is the same as rolling back a microservice—just redeploy the old Docker image.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Rolling back the code does not undo data already written by the bad version. You must also identify the affected partitions, restore them from the blue table or a snapshot, and potentially reprocess downstream tables. Safe deploy patterns (blue-green, canary) prevent bad writes from reaching production in the first place.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Adding a new column to a table is always backward compatible and safe to deploy without testing.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Adding a NOT NULL column without a default value breaks existing INSERT statements from old pipeline code still running in parallel. Adding a column with a different name than expected by downstream dbt models causes silent nulls. Schema changes must be validated against all consumers and always use nullable columns with defaults during the transition.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Feature flags are only for web applications, not data pipelines.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Feature flags are highly effective for data pipelines. They allow new transformation logic to be deployed to production in a dormant state, validated against a single tenant or partition, and then gradually enabled—without requiring a redeployment for each activation step.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Blue-green environments for petabyte-scale tables rely on copy-on-write metadata (Iceberg, Delta, Snowflake zero-copy clone) rather than physical data duplication, keeping the cost proportional to metadata and newly written files rather than the full table size.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Rollback triggers must be automated and not depend on human alerting response; define explicit SLO thresholds for output quality (null rates, row count deltas, aggregate divergence) and wire them to automated swap-revert playbooks.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Retain the blue environment for at least 48 hours post-swap to allow detection of issues that appear only after a full business cycle. Use Iceberg time travel or Delta history to restore individual partitions without reverting the entire table.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Instrument every pipeline with output quality metrics emitted to Prometheus: row_count, null_rate per key column, max_event_timestamp, records_late_pct. Alert on post-deploy deviations, not just absolute thresholds.
productionConsiderations.security: Blue-green environments should inherit the same IAM policies and row-level security rules as the production environment. Validate security policies as part of the green environment build, not after the swap.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Use warehouse-native zero-copy clones (Snowflake CREATE TABLE ... CLONE, Iceberg branch) to avoid doubling storage costs during the hold period. Set automatic cleanup policies to delete stale blue environments after the hold period expires.
productionConsiderations.performance: Output-divergence checks should query only the canary partition rather than full tables to keep CI/CD wall time under 10 minutes. Pre-compute comparison aggregates in the pipeline itself rather than running a separate comparison job.

codeExamples.title: Blue-Green Atomic Table Swap with Snowflake and Output Divergence Check
codeExamples.overview: A Python script orchestrated as an Airflow task that builds a new version of a revenue table in a green schema, runs quality and divergence checks against the production (blue) table, and performs an atomic SWAP TABLE if checks pass. On failure, the script logs the regression and leaves blue intact.
codeExamples.code:
import snowflake.connector
import logging
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Optional

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@dataclass
class DivergenceResult:
    passed: bool
    blue_rows: int
    green_rows: int
    row_delta_pct: float
    blue_revenue: float
    green_revenue: float
    revenue_delta_pct: float
    details: str

def run_blue_green_swap(
    conn: snowflake.connector.SnowflakeConnection,
    blue_table: str = "ANALYTICS.PROD.REVENUE_ATTRIBUTION",
    green_table: str = "ANALYTICS.STAGING.REVENUE_ATTRIBUTION_GREEN",
    max_row_delta_pct: float = 2.0,
    max_revenue_delta_pct: float = 0.5,
) -> bool:
    """
    1. Run divergence checks between green (new) and blue (current prod) table.
    2. If checks pass, perform atomic SWAP TABLE.
    3. Rename old blue to _blue_backup for 48-hour hold.
    Returns True on successful swap, raises on failure.
    """
    cursor = conn.cursor()

    # ---- Divergence check query ----
    divergence_sql = f"""
    SELECT
        b.row_count                          AS blue_rows,
        g.row_count                          AS green_rows,
        ABS(g.row_count - b.row_count)
            / NULLIF(b.row_count, 0) * 100   AS row_delta_pct,
        b.total_revenue                      AS blue_revenue,
        g.total_revenue                      AS green_revenue,
        ABS(g.total_revenue - b.total_revenue)
            / NULLIF(ABS(b.total_revenue), 0) * 100 AS revenue_delta_pct
    FROM (
        SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count, SUM(attributed_revenue) AS total_revenue
        FROM {blue_table}
        WHERE partition_date = CURRENT_DATE - 1
    ) b
    CROSS JOIN (
        SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count, SUM(attributed_revenue) AS total_revenue
        FROM {green_table}
        WHERE partition_date = CURRENT_DATE - 1
    ) g
    """

    cursor.execute(divergence_sql)
    row = cursor.fetchone()
    result = DivergenceResult(
        passed=False,
        blue_rows=row[0], green_rows=row[1], row_delta_pct=row[2] or 0.0,
        blue_revenue=row[3], green_revenue=row[4], revenue_delta_pct=row[5] or 0.0,
        details="",
    )

    failures = []
    if result.row_delta_pct > max_row_delta_pct:
        failures.append(
            f"row_delta={result.row_delta_pct:.2f}% > threshold {max_row_delta_pct}%"
        )
    if result.revenue_delta_pct > max_revenue_delta_pct:
        failures.append(
            f"revenue_delta={result.revenue_delta_pct:.4f}% > threshold {max_revenue_delta_pct}%"
        )

    if failures:
        result.details = "; ".join(failures)
        log.error("Divergence check FAILED: %s", result.details)
        log.error("Blue rows=%d, Green rows=%d", result.blue_rows, result.green_rows)
        log.error("Blue revenue=%.2f, Green revenue=%.2f",
                  result.blue_revenue, result.green_revenue)
        raise RuntimeError(f"Blue-green swap aborted: {result.details}")

    result.passed = True
    log.info("Divergence check PASSED: row_delta=%.2f%%, revenue_delta=%.4f%%",
             result.row_delta_pct, result.revenue_delta_pct)

    # ---- Atomic swap ----
    # Step 1: Rename current blue to backup (holds it for 48h rollback window)
    backup_name = f"{blue_table}_BLUE_BACKUP"
    cursor.execute(f"ALTER TABLE {blue_table} RENAME TO {backup_name}")
    log.info("Renamed blue table to backup: %s", backup_name)

    # Step 2: Rename green to production name (atomic at catalog level)
    cursor.execute(f"ALTER TABLE {green_table} RENAME TO {blue_table}")
    log.info("Promoted green table to production: %s", blue_table)

    return True


def rollback_swap(
    conn: snowflake.connector.SnowflakeConnection,
    blue_table: str = "ANALYTICS.PROD.REVENUE_ATTRIBUTION",
) -> None:
    """Emergency rollback: swap production back to backup."""
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    backup_name = f"{blue_table}_BLUE_BACKUP"
    # Move bad green out of the way
    cursor.execute(f"ALTER TABLE {blue_table} RENAME TO {blue_table}_BAD_DEPLOY")
    # Restore backup
    cursor.execute(f"ALTER TABLE {backup_name} RENAME TO {blue_table}")
    log.warning("ROLLBACK COMPLETE: restored %s from %s", blue_table, backup_name)
codeExamples.breakdown: The run_blue_green_swap function first computes row count and revenue aggregate deltas between the green (new) and blue (current production) tables using a single CROSS JOIN query on yesterday's partition—keeping the check fast even on large tables. Divergence thresholds of 2% row delta and 0.5% revenue delta are configurable per pipeline sensitivity. If either threshold is breached, the function raises before touching the production table, leaving blue intact. The swap itself is two sequential RENAME operations which are atomic at the Snowflake catalog level. The rollback_swap function can be called by a monitoring alert or manually by an on-call engineer to restore production within seconds.

codeExamples.commonIssues: Comparing different partitions between blue and green (e.g., if green was built on a different date range); revenue delta being large due to legitimate business change (use relative thresholds and document expected changes in the PR); backup table accumulating if cleanup automation is not run.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: For very large tables, run the divergence check on a sampled or aggregated view rather than the full partition. Use Snowflake QUERY_ACCELERATION_SERVICE for the divergence query if the partition is multi-billion rows. Automate backup cleanup with a scheduled Airflow DAG that drops tables older than 72 hours.

codeExamples.title: Confluent Schema Registry Compatibility Check in CI/CD Pipeline
codeExamples.overview: A Python script run as a GitHub Actions step that submits a new Avro schema to the Confluent Schema Registry compatibility check endpoint before merging. Blocks the PR if the schema is not backward compatible, preventing breaking Kafka consumer deploys.
codeExamples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""schema_compat_check.py — run in CI before merging schema changes.

Usage:
  python schema_compat_check.py \\
    --subject orders-value \\
    --schema-file schemas/orders_v3.avsc \\
    --registry-url https://schema-registry.internal:8081 \\
    --compatibility BACKWARD
"""
import argparse
import json
import sys
import requests

AVRO_CONTENT_TYPE = "application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json"


def check_compatibility(
    registry_url: str,
    subject: str,
    schema_str: str,
    compatibility: str = "BACKWARD",
) -> bool:
    """Returns True if schema is compatible, False otherwise."""
    # First, ensure the subject has the right compatibility mode set
    config_url = f"{registry_url}/config/{subject}"
    resp = requests.put(
        config_url,
        json={"compatibility": compatibility},
        headers={"Content-Type": AVRO_CONTENT_TYPE},
        timeout=10,
    )
    resp.raise_for_status()

    # Submit schema for compatibility test against all registered versions
    test_url = f"{registry_url}/compatibility/subjects/{subject}/versions/latest"
    payload = {"schema": schema_str}
    resp = requests.post(
        test_url,
        data=json.dumps(payload),
        headers={"Content-Type": AVRO_CONTENT_TYPE},
        timeout=10,
    )

    if resp.status_code == 404:
        # No existing schema — first registration is always compatible
        print(f"No existing schema for subject '{subject}'. First registration — OK.")
        return True

    resp.raise_for_status()
    result = resp.json()
    return result.get("is_compatible", False)


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--subject", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--schema-file", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--registry-url", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--compatibility", default="BACKWARD")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    with open(args.schema_file) as f:
        # Schema Registry expects the schema as a JSON-encoded string
        schema_obj = json.load(f)
        schema_str = json.dumps(schema_obj)

    print(f"Checking {args.compatibility} compatibility for subject '{args.subject}'...")
    print(f"Schema file: {args.schema_file}")

    compatible = check_compatibility(
        registry_url=args.registry_url,
        subject=args.subject,
        schema_str=schema_str,
        compatibility=args.compatibility,
    )

    if compatible:
        print(f"COMPATIBLE: schema passes {args.compatibility} compatibility check.")
        sys.exit(0)
    else:
        print(
            f"INCOMPATIBLE: schema FAILS {args.compatibility} compatibility check.",
            file=sys.stderr,
        )
        print(
            "Breaking changes detected. Review: renamed fields, deleted fields, "
            "changed types, or removed enum values are not backward compatible.",
            file=sys.stderr,
        )
        sys.exit(1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
codeExamples.breakdown: The script first sets the subject's compatibility mode via the Schema Registry config endpoint (PUT /config/{subject}), ensuring the mode is enforced at the registry level regardless of producer settings. It then POSTs the candidate schema to /compatibility/subjects/{subject}/versions/latest which returns {is_compatible: true/false} without registering the schema. A 404 on the latest version endpoint means no schema exists yet, which is always compatible. The script exits with code 1 on incompatibility, blocking the CI pipeline and the PR merge. This is wired into GitHub Actions as a required status check.

Schema file: schemas/orders_v3.avsc
COMPATIBLE: schema passes BACKWARD compatibility check.

Incompatible schema (removed a required field):
Checking BACKWARD compatibility for subject 'orders-value'...
INCOMPATIBLE: schema FAILS BACKWARD compatibility check.

(exits with code 1, blocking the PR merge)
codeExamples.commonIssues: Schema Registry not reachable from CI runners (use internal DNS or VPN tunnel); forgetting to set the compatibility mode before the check so the registry uses a different default; checking only the latest version when FULL_TRANSITIVE compatibility requires checking against all versions.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Cache the schema registry URL and auth token in GitHub Actions secrets. Run compatibility checks in parallel for multiple schema subjects in the same PR. Consider using the Confluent Schema Registry Maven plugin for JVM-based producers, which integrates natively with the build lifecycle.

codeExamples.title: Airflow DAG Versioning Pattern with Canary Partition Validation
codeExamples.overview: An Airflow DAG implementation that deploys a new version of a Spark ETL job in canary mode: processes only yesterday's partition through new code, runs Great Expectations on both outputs, and promotes to full production only if the canary divergence check passes. Includes rollback via XCom-signaled DAG pause.
codeExamples.code:
"""revenue_etl_v2.py — versioned Airflow DAG with canary partition deploy."""
from __future__ import annotations
import pendulum
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator, BranchPythonOperator
from airflow.operators.bash import BashOperator
from airflow.models import Variable
from airflow.utils.trigger_rule import TriggerRule
import subprocess
import logging

log = logging.getLogger(__name__)

DAG_ID = "revenue_etl_v2"         # Versioned DAG ID — old v1 DAG runs in parallel
CANARY_PARTITION = "{{ ds }}"      # Only yesterday's partition runs through new code
SPARK_SUBMIT = "/usr/bin/spark-submit"
JOB_JAR = "/opt/spark-jobs/revenue-etl-2.0.jar"
GE_CHECKPOINT_V1 = "revenue_v1_checkpoint"
GE_CHECKPOINT_V2 = "revenue_v2_checkpoint"


def run_spark_canary(partition_date: str, **_):
    """Submit new Spark job for canary partition only."""
    cmd = [
        SPARK_SUBMIT,
        "--master", "k8s://https://k8s-master:6443",
        "--conf", "spark.executor.instances=20",
        "--conf", f"spark.app.name=revenue_etl_v2_canary_{partition_date}",
        JOB_JAR,
        "--partition", partition_date,
        "--output-table", f"ANALYTICS.STAGING.REVENUE_V2_CANARY_{partition_date.replace('-', '_')}",
    ]
    log.info("Running canary Spark job: %s", " ".join(cmd))
    result = subprocess.run(cmd, capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
    log.info(result.stdout)


def check_canary_divergence(partition_date: str, **context):
    """Compare canary output to production v1 output for the same partition.
    Returns 'promote' or 'rollback' branch task ID.
    """
    import snowflake.connector
    conn = snowflake.connector.connect(
        account=Variable.get("snowflake_account"),
        user=Variable.get("snowflake_user"),
        password=Variable.get("snowflake_password"),
        role="ETL_ROLE",
        warehouse="ETL_WH",
    )
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    cursor.execute(f"""
        SELECT
            ABS(v2.rc - v1.rc) / NULLIF(v1.rc, 0) * 100 AS row_delta_pct,
            ABS(v2.rev - v1.rev) / NULLIF(ABS(v1.rev), 0) * 100 AS rev_delta_pct
        FROM
            (SELECT COUNT(*) rc, SUM(revenue) rev
             FROM ANALYTICS.PROD.REVENUE_ATTRIBUTION
             WHERE partition_date = '{partition_date}') v1
        CROSS JOIN
            (SELECT COUNT(*) rc, SUM(revenue) rev
             FROM ANALYTICS.STAGING.REVENUE_V2_CANARY_{partition_date.replace('-', '_')}
             WHERE partition_date = '{partition_date}') v2
    """)
    row_delta_pct, rev_delta_pct = cursor.fetchone()
    conn.close()

    log.info("Canary divergence: row_delta=%.2f%%, rev_delta=%.4f%%",
             row_delta_pct or 0, rev_delta_pct or 0)

    if (row_delta_pct or 0) > 2.0 or (rev_delta_pct or 0) > 0.5:
        log.error("Canary divergence EXCEEDS threshold — triggering rollback branch")
        context["ti"].xcom_push(key="canary_fail_reason",
                                 value=f"row_delta={row_delta_pct:.2f}%, rev_delta={rev_delta_pct:.4f}%")
        return "rollback_and_alert"
    return "promote_to_production"


def promote_to_production(partition_date: str, **_):
    """Backfill all partitions with new code and swap production table."""
    log.info("Canary PASSED. Promoting v2 to production for all partitions.")
    # In practice: submit backfill Spark job for remaining date range,
    # then call run_blue_green_swap() from the earlier example.


def rollback_and_alert(**context):
    reason = context["ti"].xcom_pull(key="canary_fail_reason", task_ids="check_canary_divergence")
    log.error("ROLLBACK triggered. Reason: %s", reason)
    # Drop canary table, keep v1 DAG running, page on-call via PagerDuty API
    raise RuntimeError(f"Canary deploy rolled back: {reason}")


with DAG(
    dag_id=DAG_ID,
    start_date=pendulum.datetime(2024, 1, 1, tz="UTC"),
    schedule="0 6 * * *",
    catchup=False,
    tags=["revenue", "canary", "v2"],
    default_args={"retries": 1, "retry_delay": pendulum.duration(minutes=5)},
) as dag:

    run_canary = PythonOperator(
        task_id="run_spark_canary",
        python_callable=run_spark_canary,
        op_kwargs={"partition_date": "{{ ds }}"},
    )

    divergence_check = BranchPythonOperator(
        task_id="check_canary_divergence",
        python_callable=check_canary_divergence,
        op_kwargs={"partition_date": "{{ ds }}"},
    )

    promote = PythonOperator(
        task_id="promote_to_production",
        python_callable=promote_to_production,
        op_kwargs={"partition_date": "{{ ds }}"},
    )

    rollback = PythonOperator(
        task_id="rollback_and_alert",
        python_callable=rollback_and_alert,
        trigger_rule=TriggerRule.NONE_FAILED,
    )

    run_canary >> divergence_check >> [promote, rollback]
codeExamples.breakdown: The DAG uses a versioned DAG ID (revenue_etl_v2) so both v1 and v2 can run simultaneously without Airflow treating them as the same pipeline. The BranchPythonOperator implements the canary decision gate: it runs the divergence check and returns the task_id of the next task to execute (promote_to_production or rollback_and_alert), skipping the other branch. XCom is used to pass the failure reason from the divergence check to the rollback task. The TriggerRule.NONE_FAILED on the rollback task ensures it only fires when explicitly selected by the branch. The v1 DAG continues running until the v2 DAG has successfully processed all partitions and the swap is complete.
